assumptions: The alert's one-second open-to-close span is assumed to reflect only how long the alert condition was observed, not the duration of any customer-facing impact; actual impact is unknown.
Customer impact is assumed unknown rather than zero — the absence of metrics is not evidence that nothing broke.

It is assumed, but not verified, that the metrics query was aimed at the correct service and time window; an empty result could equally indicate a query/anchoring fault or a gap in the metrics pipeline.
No logs were examined, so nothing about the service's internal behaviour during the window has been ruled in or out.
input.executive_summary: An automated alert reported an elevated rate of errors on one internal service. The alert opened and closed within about a second, and an automated responder began investigating immediately. When it tried to retrieve the service's recent performance data for the period in question, none came back, so it could not confirm whether customers experienced any failures, how many, or for how long. With no evidence to work from, the responder made no changes to the service and handed the incident to a human on-call engineer. No fix was applied because no problem was ever confirmed; what is known is that the monitoring data needed to answer that question was unavailable.
input.root_cause: Not determined. The HighErrorRate alert on io-shop fired and was picked up, but the investigating agent's query for the service's per-minute metrics anchored on 15:29 returned zero minutes of data, so there was no evidence to distinguish a real error spike from an alerting or metrics-pipeline artifact; no logs were read and no remediation was attempted before the incident was escalated. The only open question worth chasing first is why the metrics read came back empty — that gap is itself either the cause of a spurious alert or the reason a genuine one could not be diagnosed.
